title: Police: Officers fatally shot London man for nearby kids' safety
article: Concerned for the safety of the two children in the room, officers shot a hatchet-wielding Samuel Maloney until he dropped to the ground, London police say in response to a $17-million lawsuit from the dead man's widow.

Police fatally shot Maloney, 35, during a pre-dawn raid on his Old South home on Dec. 23, 2016 , after he fired a crossbow at an officer and charged at others armed with a hatchet, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said in a report last year clearing the officers involved of any wrongdoing.

"In response to this attack, and out of concern for the safety and welfare of the children in the home . . . members of the LPS discharged their weapons until the attack was stopped," says a statement of defence from police to the lawsuit.

Maloney's widow, Melissa Facciolo, filed a lawsuit in December alleging police should have known the early-morning police raid on the family home at 35 Duchess Ave., where the couple's two young children were inside, could have resulted in serious injury or death.

The lawsuit against the police services board, Chief John Pare and 10 unnamed officers also takes aim at the warrant that brought police to the house two days before Christmas, saying it didn't include vital information about Maloney's history of violence, the possibility of weapons in the home and that children would likely be there.

But police say they were aware of the couple's record for violence and weapons, Maloney's anti-authority attitude and the likelihood of weapons inside the home, the statement of defence says.

No reason was given why that information wasn't included in the search warrant application, written by an officer who had never completed one before, said the SIU report that criticized London police over the warrant's contents.
Police launched an investigation into offensive social media posts attributed to Maloney on Dec. 5, 2016 , the statement of defence says.
Statements of claim, and defences filed in response, include allegations not yet tested in court.

Police obtained a warrant on Dec. 21 to search Maloney's home weeks after a manifesto that included anti-Semitic material was sent to newsletter subscribers at the Hyland Cinema, where Facciolo managed the theatre's website and sent out email bulletins and Maloney was helping develop its software, the SIU report said .

Police planned to arrest Maloney when he left his house, but they decided to force their way inside to carry out the search warrant after he didn't come out in two days. Officers announced their purpose for being inside, the statement of defence says, noting Maloney knew about the police presence from a surveillance system.
Police found Maloney and Facciolo in a room, where Maloney fired a crossbow at an officer, prompting the officer to return fire, leaving both injured, the statement of defence says.
" . . . Prior to firing the crossbow Maloney had contacted a lawyer and discussed . . . matters concerning the LPS entering the house and stating that they had a warrant," the documents say.

London criminal lawyer Nick Cake previously told the Free Press Maloney, one of his clients, called him shortly after 6 a.m. saying police were raiding his home. Cake described hearing a man yelling and Facciolo screaming before four gunshots rang out.
Cake, who rushed to the scene, declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday.
Maloney's father, Peter, also previously told the Free Press his son called him as police were entering his home, though neither the lawsuit nor the SIU report makes any mention of the call.

The officer struck by the crossbow fired three shots, striking Maloney once in the shoulder. Facciolo ran to a rear bedroom, where two officers were inside with the couple's two young children, while police ordered Maloney out of the room with his hands up, the SIU report said.
"Instead, Maloney armed himself with a hatchet. A firearm also later was found in a location available to Maloney," the statement of defence alleges.

Maloney ran for the bedroom where the officers and his family were holed up. One of the officers fired five shots from his submachine-gun at Maloney, striking him three times in the chest. Maloney fell to the ground near the bedroom door before the third officer shot him once in the head, the SIU report said.

Facciolo's lawsuit, which makes no mention of the hatchet, alleges police shot Maloney in the head after he already was dead. The lawsuit seeks damages for lost income for both Facciolo and Maloney, expenses related to his death and compensation for future losses of support, companionship and care.

The statement of defence denies Facciolo has suffered any special damages, arguing the officers' actions were reasonably necessary based on the circumstances. Police, contacted Thursday, declined to comment while the case if before the courts.

Facciolo , who still lives in the single-story home where her husband died, was charged with eight weapons and drug offences in the wake of the shooting. She pleaded guilty to possession of a prohibited weapon in last spring and was given 12 months' probation and a lifetime weapons ban. The other charges were withdrawn
